title: Release Barabbas (Luke 23:13–25)
hook: Pilate says three times he finds no fault, and yields to the shouts

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's laughter, and a man who would not perform. Your line was he answered nothing. Which jab did you let go by? Day five hundred eighty-four.

You've seen it happen in a meeting. Someone in charge knows the right answer. They even say it out loud. Then the room gets loud, and the pressure builds, and twenty minutes later they announce the opposite. Nobody changed their mind with an argument. They just got tired of the noise. Jesus is back from Herod, still in the gorgeous robe. Pilate calls together the chief priests, the rulers and the people, and gives his verdict, the verdict of the most powerful man in the city. What happens next is a story about what a verdict is worth when the room is loud.

Pilate says it plainly: I've examined him, and I find no fault in him. Neither did Herod. I'll have him beaten, and let him go. And the crowd in front of him cries out, all together, away with this man, release unto us Barabbas. Luke tells us who Barabbas is: a man thrown in prison for an uprising in the city, and for murder. Pilate speaks to them again, wanting to release Jesus. They shout, crucify him. Then, in the King James words: "And he said unto them the third time, Why, what evil hath he done? I have found no cause of death in him: I will therefore chastise him, and let him go." Three times, no fault. Luke counts them so you'll notice. "And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." The voices prevailed. Not the evidence. Not the law. The volume. Pilate releases the man jailed for murder, and hands Jesus over to their will. Two things are worth holding carefully here. First, this is a crowd in a courtyard on one morning, with its leaders, not a whole people. Christians in the past used scenes like this to blame the Jewish people for Jesus's death, with terrible results, and churches across the traditions now reject that reading. The sentence was Rome's, and the cross was a Roman punishment. Second, the man with the power knew the truth, said it three times, and gave it up. Barabbas, by the way, is Aramaic: bar Abba, son of the father.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE OF DEATH IN HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't yield to one loud crowd. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you know is right, or true, that you've gone quiet about because people around you are loud. At work, in your family, online, in your own head. Say it to yourself plainly, once. Then a second time. Then a third. Notice whether it still feels true. You don't have to fight anyone today. Just don't hand it over. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Release Barabbas. The crowd's cry before Pilate: free the man jailed for uprising and murder, and crucify the one the governor found innocent.
Your line: three times, no fault. Today, when the room gets loud, say the true thing you know one more time, calmly, before you let it go. Day five hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Christians hear the trial before Pilate read aloud on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, often with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that everyone takes part in the shout rather than blaming others.

fork.setup: you're the governor. you've said three times the man is innocent. the crowd is shouting louder. what do you do?
options: release him, as your verdict says.
give the crowd what it wants.
send him back to Herod again.
fork.reveal: "the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed." Pilate releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to their will.

original.note: Greek spelling of an Aramaic name, bar Abba: son of the father.

trapdoor: what you thought: the crowd chose a criminal over Jesus.
what it means: the man with power found no fault three times, and still gave way to the loudest voices.
what a scholar hears: Barabbas is Aramaic for son of the father; Luke stresses the threefold innocence verdict; and the sentence of crucifixion was Rome's.

notes: Luke 23:17 (the custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast) is missing from many early manuscripts; the script doesn't rely on it.
Rejection of collective Jewish blame: e.g. the Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) and statements by many Protestant and Orthodox bodies. Phrased generally; confirm.
Barabbas from Aramaic bar Abba, 'son of the father': commonly given etymology. Confirm.
howItsDone describes congregations reading the crowd's lines in Palm Sunday and Good Friday Passion readings; confirm this is accurate for many churches.
